before.content_html:
What Is Computational Thinking?

Computational thinking is a structured way of approaching problems so they can be solved clearly and efficiently. It is not about using a computer — it is about thinking in a way that makes complex problems manageable. Two key techniques are decomposition and abstraction. Together, they form the foundation of everything you will study in GCSE Computer Science.

Key Fact

An algorithm is a sequence of steps that can be followed to complete a task. A computer program is an implementation of an algorithm in a specific programming language. The algorithm is the abstract plan; the program is the working code.

Algorithms: Sequence Matters

The word “sequence” is deliberate. An algorithm is not simply a “set” of instructions — a set has no order. An algorithm’s steps must be followed in the right order to reach the correct result. A recipe is an everyday example: if you add the eggs before the flour, you do not get the same result.

Every algorithm can be expressed in different forms: as pseudo-code, as a flowchart, or as actual program code. You need to be comfortable moving between all three representations.

Decomposition

Decomposition means breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems. Each sub-problem accomplishes a specific, identifiable task. Sub-problems can themselves be further broken down, creating a hierarchy of manageable tasks.

Consider building a mobile banking app. At the top level it is one enormous problem. Decomposed, it becomes: user authentication, account balance display, payment processing, transaction history, and security alerts. Each of those can be decomposed further — payment processing breaks into input validation, fraud checks, bank transfer protocols, and confirmation messages. Each piece is now small enough for a developer (or a team) to tackle independently.

Suppose you are asked to build an online GP appointment booking system. Decomposing it gives at least four sub-problems:

  • Patient login — verify identity securely
  • Show available slots — fetch free appointment times from the database
  • Book slot — write the booking and prevent double-booking
  • Send confirmation — email or SMS reminder to the patient

Each sub-problem is now small enough to design, code and test independently. A team could work on all four simultaneously.

Abstraction

Abstraction means removing unnecessary detail so that you can focus on the information that actually matters. It is not about making things simpler than they are — it is about identifying which details are relevant and filtering out everything else.

The London Underground map is a classic example. Real tube lines curve, dip underground, and vary in spacing. A geographically accurate map would be too cluttered to use. The Underground map abstracts away distances and precise geography, keeping only the connections between stations and their order. That is all a passenger needs to plan a journey.

Key Fact

In programming, abstraction happens constantly. A variable named playerScore hides the actual memory address where the value is stored. A function called sendNotification() hides dozens of lines of networking code behind a single meaningful name. Programmers use abstraction to manage complexity at every scale.

Levels of Abstraction

Abstraction works at multiple levels. A sat-nav system abstracts away the physics of road surfaces, the full text of the Highway Code, and the mechanical workings of your car. It retains only: current position, destination, road network connections, and estimated speeds. The less detail the system has to process, the faster and clearer the route calculation.

Similarly, when you design an algorithm you make abstraction decisions: what are the inputs? What processing happens on them? What are the outputs? Everything else — the hardware it runs on, the user interface colour scheme — is abstracted away from the algorithm itself.

A school login system can be decomposed and abstracted as follows:

Decomposition: (1) Get username and password. (2) Check against stored records. (3) Either grant access or display an error.

Abstraction applied: The algorithm does not need to know how passwords are stored in the database, what operating system the server runs, or how the network packet gets from the student’s laptop to the server. It only needs: username, password, stored credentials, and a match/no-match decision.

Inputs: username, password. Processing: compare input to stored values. Output: “Access granted” or “Access denied.”

Why These Skills Matter

Decomposition and abstraction are not just theory — they are the practical habits of every professional software developer. When engineers at a social media company build a new feature for hundreds of millions of users, they start by decomposing the requirement into sub-tasks and abstracting away the hardware and infrastructure concerns. The same thinking applies when you write even a short program in school.

In your exam, you may be asked to explain what decomposition or abstraction means, apply them to a given scenario, or identify where they appear in a described system. Always ground your answer in the specific problem given — examiners reward precise application, not generic definitions.

lessons.title: Representing Algorithms: Pseudo-code, Flowcharts and Trace Tables

before.content_html:
Three Ways to Write an Algorithm

Once you have designed an algorithm using decomposition and abstraction, you need a way to write it down clearly. There are three standard representations: pseudo-code, flowcharts, and actual program code. Your exam may ask you to read, complete or write in any of these forms — always check what format the question requires before answering.

Key Fact

Standard flowchart symbols: oval/rounded rectangle (start or stop), rectangle (process or action), diamond (decision — has yes/no exits), parallelogram (input or output). Arrows show the direction of flow.

Flowcharts

A flowchart gives you a visual picture of how an algorithm flows. Every step is drawn as a shape; arrows connect them in order. The diamond shape is particularly important — it represents a decision with two exits (usually labelled Yes and No). Decisions are used to model selection (if/else) and the loop condition in iteration. A flowchart for a loop has an arrow that curves back upward from the “No” exit of the diamond to an earlier step.

In an exam you might be asked to trace through a flowchart and state its output, add a missing shape, or correct an error. Always follow the arrows carefully — it is easy to take the wrong branch from a diamond.

AQA Standard Pseudo-code

Your exam will always present pseudo-code questions using the current version of the AQA standard pseudo-code. You must be able to read and write it confidently. The key constructs are shown below. Note that AQA uses ← for assignment (not =), and keywords such as THEN, ENDIF, ENDWHILE, ENDFOR, UNTIL that clearly mark where structures end.

Assignment:
score ← 0
The arrow means “assign the value on the right to the variable on the left.”

Output:
OUTPUT score

Input:
name ← USERINPUT

Selection (IF):
IF score >= 50 THEN
  OUTPUT “Pass”
ELSE
  OUTPUT “Fail”
ENDIF

Count-controlled loop (FOR):
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
  OUTPUT i
ENDFOR

Condition-controlled loop (WHILE):
WHILE answer ≠ “quit”
  answer ← USERINPUT
ENDWHILE

Condition-controlled loop (REPEAT…UNTIL):
REPEAT
  answer ← USERINPUT
UNTIL answer = “quit”
The condition is checked after each iteration, so the body always runs at least once.

Key Fact

AQA pseudo-code uses ← for assignment and requires closing keywords: ENDIF, ENDWHILE, ENDFOR. The REPEAT…UNTIL loop always executes its body at least once because the condition is tested after the body runs — unlike WHILE, which tests the condition first.

Trace Tables

A trace table is used to track the values of variables as an algorithm runs. Each column represents a variable (or the output); each row records the variable values after one execution step. Trace tables let you check whether an algorithm produces the correct output and are the standard method for finding logic errors.

In the exam, trace-table questions are worth 4 marks and are one of the most commonly dropped mark areas. The two most frequent errors are: adding extra rows (tracing steps that didn’t actually happen), and forgetting to update a counter or comparison variable on every iteration.

Consider this AQA pseudo-code algorithm:

total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 4
  total ← total + i
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total

Trace table (columns: i, total, OUTPUT):

Before loop: total = 0

i = 1: total = 0 + 1 = 1

i = 2: total = 1 + 2 = 3

i = 3: total = 3 + 3 = 6

i = 4: total = 6 + 4 = 10

Loop ends (i would be 5, greater than 4). OUTPUT: 10

The algorithm adds the integers 1 to 4 and outputs their sum. Its purpose: sum the integers from 1 to n (here n=4).

Determining the Purpose of an Algorithm

After completing a trace table, you should be able to describe what the algorithm does. Rather than just listing the outputs, identify the pattern: is it counting, summing, searching, filtering? A well-worded purpose statement names the inputs, describes the processing, and states the outputs.

For example: “The algorithm takes a list of names as input, searches through them one by one (processing), and outputs the position of a target name if found.” This is clearer than “it finds a name.”

For simpler algorithms, visual inspection — reading through the code and reasoning about what it does — is faster than filling a full trace table. Look for: the loop condition (to know when the loop stops), which variables are updated in the loop body, and what is outputted. Visual inspection saves time on short sequences; trace tables are safer for anything involving nested loops or complex conditions.
before.exam_tip_html: For trace-table questions (4 marks), complete every cell for every iteration — do not leave blank cells for values that did not change. Only add a new row when the algorithm actually executes another step; never add extra rows for iterations the loop does not perform. For ‘state the purpose’ questions, name the inputs, the operation performed, and the output — a one-line description that is specific to the algorithm shown, not a generic “it processes data.”

lessons.title: Searching Algorithms: Linear and Binary Search

before.exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark ‘Compare and Contrast’ question on linear versus binary search, structure your answer as direct comparisons, not two separate lists. For example: “Linear search works on unsorted data, whereas binary search requires sorted data.” Each paired comparison earns more marks than describing one algorithm then the other separately. Always include the time efficiency comparison (binary search is faster for large lists) and the sorted-data requirement for binary search.

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort and Merge Sort

before.exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark ‘Compare and Contrast’ question on bubble sort versus merge sort, structure your answer as direct paired comparisons. For example: “Bubble sort is simple to implement, whereas merge sort is more complex but considerably faster for large datasets.” Avoid listing all of bubble sort’s features then all of merge sort’s — direct comparisons earn more marks. Always address: how each algorithm works, time efficiency, memory use, and a conclusion about which is suited to which scenario.
before.content_html:
Why Sort Data?

Sorting data into order is a fundamental computing task. Binary search requires sorted data. Databases display results in a meaningful order. A music app shows albums alphabetically. A leaderboard ranks scores from highest to lowest. The specification requires you to know two sorting algorithms: bubble sort and merge sort. You must understand how each works and be able to compare them.

Bubble Sort

Bubble sort works by repeatedly comparing adjacent pairs of items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. After the first pass, the largest item has “bubbled” to the last position. After the second pass, the second largest is in place. The algorithm continues until a complete pass produces no swaps — which means the list is sorted.

The mechanics, step by step: Compare items at positions 1 and 2 — swap if needed. Compare positions 2 and 3 — swap if needed. Continue to the end of the list. That completes one pass. Repeat passes until no swaps occur.

Key Fact

Advantages of bubble sort: Simple to understand and implement. Sorts in place (no extra memory needed). Can detect an already-sorted list early (zero swaps on the first pass). Disadvantages: Very slow for large datasets — many passes and many comparisons are needed. Inefficient even in the average case.

Start: [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]

Pass 1:
Compare 5,3 → swap → [3, 5, 8, 1, 4]
Compare 5,8 → no swap → [3, 5, 8, 1, 4]
Compare 8,1 → swap → [3, 5, 1, 8, 4]
Compare 8,4 → swap → [3, 5, 1, 4, 8]
End of pass 1: largest item (8) is now in position 5.

Pass 2:
Compare 3,5 → no swap
Compare 5,1 → swap → [3, 1, 5, 4, 8]
Compare 5,4 → swap → [3, 1, 4, 5, 8]
End of pass 2: [3, 1, 4, 5, 8]

Pass 3:
Compare 3,1 → swap → [1, 3, 4, 5, 8]
Compare 3,4 → no swap
End of pass 3: [1, 3, 4, 5, 8]

Pass 4: No swaps — list is sorted. Algorithm stops. Final list: [1, 3, 4, 5, 8]

Merge Sort

Merge sort uses a divide-and-conquer approach. It repeatedly splits the list in half until each sub-list contains a single item. A list of one item is inherently sorted. It then merges pairs of sub-lists back together, placing items in the correct order during each merge. The merge phase is where the actual sorting happens.

Split phase:
Pass 1: [38, 27, 43, 3] and [9, 82, 10]
Pass 2: [38, 27] | [43, 3] | [9, 82] | [10]
Pass 3: [38] | [27] | [43] | [3] | [9] | [82] | [10]

Merge phase (working back up):
Merge [38] and [27] → [27, 38]
Merge [43] and [3] → [3, 43]
Merge [9] and [82] → [9, 82]
[10] remains [10]

Merge [27, 38] and [3, 43] → [3, 27, 38, 43]
Merge [9, 82] and [10] → [9, 10, 82]

Final merge: [3, 27, 38, 43] and [9, 10, 82] → [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]

The list is now fully sorted. Note how each merge step compares the first elements of the two sub-lists and picks the smaller one.

Key Fact

Advantages of merge sort: Much faster than bubble sort for large datasets. Consistent performance regardless of how the data is initially ordered. Disadvantages: Requires extra memory to store the temporary sub-lists during the merging process. More complex to implement than bubble sort.

Comparing Bubble Sort and Merge Sort

The two algorithms make a direct trade-off between simplicity and speed. Bubble sort is easy to code and uses no extra memory, but it becomes impractical for lists with more than a few hundred items. Merge sort is consistently fast even on very large lists, but it requires extra memory for the sub-lists and is harder to implement correctly.

As with searching algorithms, the right choice depends on the context. For a small list of exam results in a classroom app, bubble sort is perfectly adequate. For sorting millions of customer records in a bank’s database overnight, merge sort (or a similar efficient algorithm) is essential.

Bubble sort:

  • Simple to implement
  • Sorts in place — no extra memory required
  • Can detect already-sorted list early
  • Slow for large or randomly ordered data

Merge sort:

  • More complex to implement
  • Requires extra memory for sub-lists
  • Consistent performance regardless of initial order
  • Much faster for large datasets
